news.Title: 「黃仁勳調查」衝擊南亞科！一度跌停 買在8月高點者一張已虧逾30萬元
news.Content:
美國加州檢察長邦塔（Rob Bonta）19日向美媒《POLITICO》證實，目前已對AI晶片大廠輝達（Nvidia）展開正式調查。受此利空消息重擊，記憶體大廠南亞科（2408）今日股價面臨沉重賣壓，盤中一度打入跌停價264.5元，買在八月高點者，帳面每張虧損30多萬元。隨後低接買盤隨即湧入承接，推升成交量迅速放大至近5萬張，跌停隨之打開；截至目前，股價維持在265元附近震盪整理，跌幅略為收斂至9%以上，分析師表示，先別急著進場接刀。

南亞科今日盤中最低下探至264.5元，一舉跌破5月20日低點265.5元，創下近5個月來新低。回顧8月28日波段高點569元，短短不到三個月時間，股價累計跌幅已超過五成；若投資人買在最高點且抱股至今，換算下來每張帳面虧損已超過30.4萬元。

倫元投顧分析師王春盛指出，AI運算高度依賴高頻寬記憶體（HBM），一旦輝達面臨調查甚至影響晶片出貨動能，連帶將波及上游記憶體的整體需求量。觀察南亞科今日盤中重摔至跌停價264.5元，再度改寫波段新低，顯示短線市場賣壓相當沉重。

不過，王春盛也強調，回歸基本面檢視，南亞科2026年第三季單季營收達1,336.49億元，季增61.9%，毛利率高達85.7%，單季每股純益（EPS）25.4元，累計前三季EPS更達49.28元，整體獲利表現依舊亮眼。

在技術面與操作策略上，王春盛分析，目前南亞科KD指標已落入超賣區，股價跌深後確實具備醞釀技術性反彈的條件，但「超賣並不代表立即止跌」。建議手中仍持有股票的投資人不宜貿然向下攤平，應先密切觀察跌停打開後的籌碼換手與成交量能變化；至於空手者，則建議耐心等待明確止跌訊號浮現、股價重新站回短期均線後再行分批布局，切忌急著進場接刀。

輝達前執行長黃仁勳與疑似具備中國大陸間諜身分的黃樂（Alice Huang）婚外情，美國加州檢察長已展開正式調查，預計要釐清輝達的先進晶片或核心機密資訊是否因此流入中國大陸，以及該公司在相關資訊揭露上是否涉有誤導投資人與公眾之嫌。

news.Title: 1 Unstoppable Stock to Buy Before It Joins NVDA and AAPL in the $1 Trillion Club
news.Content:
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) briefly became a $1 trillion company in September, but it lost that milestone after a prolonged artificial intelligence (AI) stock correction. However, the chipmaker is set to rejoin Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) as a trillion-dollar company. These are the catalysts that can drive the stock higher.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Nvidia confusion creates an opening

AMD has been viewed as the No. 2 graphics processing unit (GPU) chipmaker for several years, with Nvidia comfortably holding on to the top spot. However, Nvidia suddenly faces significant uncertainty with former CEO Jensen Huang out of the company and angling for a comeback.

Nvidia currently doesn't seem receptive to a reunion, and that can cost the company. Some investors argue that Huang's departure will make it difficult for Nvidia to continue innovating despite the competitive edge it has already obtained.

The AI industry is moving rapidly, and leadership complexities can cost Nvidia valuable time. It can be the difference between missing out on the latest technology and watching hyperscalers turn to alternatives.

This scenario positions AMD as the chipmaker with the most to gain from the confusion, and the company has been taking major steps to close the gap. For instance, AMD is making its chip fleet more attractive by making it much easier for developers to port existing Nvidia CUDA applications to its HIP platform.

Nvidia's CUDA was previously a major moat. Moving to another software essentially meant rewriting vast amounts of code, but that's no longer the case. If AMD can win over more businesses with an easier migration, it creates more headaches for a company already full of them.

Growth was picking up before the Nvidia shake-up

Although Nvidia has captured most of the headlines throughout the AI boom, AMD has been quietly accelerating its growth. Data center revenue surged by 97% year over year in the third quarter, while overall revenue reached $13.4 billion, up by 45% year over year. That also represents a 16% sequential boost.

AMD CEO Lisa Su told investors that demand for its AI products is still accelerating. The chipmaker also remains confident that revenue growth will surge in the coming years, along with higher net profit margins.

Story Continues

AMD trades at a 30 forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which may be higher than what some investors are willing to handle. However, this same company almost doubled its net income year over year. AMD wrapped up the quarter with an 18.2% net profit margin, and if it can get closer to Nvidia's 62% net profit margin, the stock should have an easy time reclaiming a $1 trillion market cap and marching toward new highs.

news.Title: HSBC Just Turned Bullish on Cisco Stock Again. Here’s Why It Expects 40% Upside.
news.Content:
Cisco Systems (CSCO) has long worn the label of a mature networking giant, rarely linked to rapid growth. Yet now, the company is shaking up Wall Street's expectations. Fueled by a wave of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investment, strong enterprise demand, and an exceptional quarter, Cisco has prompted HSBC to abandon its cautious stance, upgrade the stock to "Buy," and raise its price target to $133.

With the bank forecasting nearly 40% upside, Cisco's growth revival is quickly becoming impossible to ignore. Let's take a closer look.

HSBC's Change of Heart Has a Clear Catalyst

On Nov. 17, HSBC raised CSCO stock to "Buy" from "Hold" and increased its price target to $133 from $120. The new target implies approximately 40% potential upside from current levels. The move is notable because HSBC had downgraded Cisco stock from "Buy" to "Hold" in August, cutting its target from $137 to $120. Its latest upgrade reverses that decision, driven by a stronger networking outlook, firmer AI-related demand, and a valuation it considers attractive relative to growth.

HSBC expects Cisco's networking revenue to compound at 19.2% annually from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2029. The firm also forecasts adjusted EPS to grow 14.9% annually from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2031. The $133 price target applies a 23 times multiple to the estimated next-12-month adjusted EPS of $5.78. In other words, the valuation depends on earnings growth continuing and investors maintaining that earnings multiple.

The Quarter Was Strong Because Demand Reached Beyond AI

Cisco's first quarter of fiscal 2027 performance encouraged HSBC to shift from caution to a more optimistic stance. The company reported $18.5 billion in revenue, up 24% year-over-year (YOY). Adjusted EPS rose 40% YOY to $1.40, while adjusted operating margin reached 37.8%. CFO Mark Patterson said the company exceeded the high end of its guidance for revenue, operating margin, and EPS. Cisco focused not just on shipping more equipment but on turning the stronger quarter into higher profitability.

Story Continues

Product revenue rose 32% YOY to $14.7 billion, while services revenue grew just 1% to $3.9 billion. Networking stole the spotlight with a remarkable 43% increase, while security, collaboration, and software each posted steady gains of 7%, 8%, and 8%, respectively, with software reaching $6.1 billion. Clearly, hardware drove this acceleration, not services.

Orders provide an important check on revenue momentum. Product orders climbed 21%, backed by double-digit growth across every region. Service provider and cloud orders soared 47%, while enterprise and public-sector orders advanced 15% and 13%. Networking orders surged 28%, marking its ninth-straight quarter of double-digit gains. This broad-based recovery reduces reliance on hyperscalers.

The order picture also extends into traditional networking. Campus networking orders increased 14%, and telecom orders rose 20%. Cisco is benefiting not only from new AI data centers but also from customers upgrading enterprise networks and connectivity. These projects can broaden the addressable demand pool and make the growth profile less dependent on the timing of a few large AI deployments.

Nonetheless, hyperscalers still remain the biggest growth catalyst. Cisco projects $9 billion in AI infrastructure sales to these customers in fiscal 2027, up from about $4 billion in fiscal 2026 and higher than its earlier $7.5 billion forecast. Management pointed to stronger orders, better visibility, and three AI design wins with Silicon One systems and 1.6-terabit optics.

Cisco ended the quarter with $46.2 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO), up 8% YOY, and annual recurring revenue (ARR) of $32.7 billion, up 4%. Subscription revenue accounted for 44% of sales. No doubt, there is a sharp gap between hardware and services growth, but these numbers also reflect a steadier revenue foundation as networking equipment demand moves through its cycle.

Upbeat Outlook Adds to the Bullish Case

Cisco raised its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $74.8 billion to $75.8 billion and adjusted EPS to $5.47 to $5.53. The revenue midpoint implies roughly 19% YOY growth. For Q2, management expects revenue of $18 billion to $18.2 billion and EPS of $1.34 to $1.36.

Yet the quarter revealed a price to pay. Adjusted gross margin edged down to 65.6%, and product gross margin slipped to 63.7%. Management pointed to a heavier hardware mix and rising memory costs, with some relief from productivity gains and pricing. The very products fueling growth are, for now, less profitable than those they are replacing. Management remains confident it will reach a 36% adjusted operating margin for fiscal 2027, up from 34.8% in fiscal 2026, suggesting productivity and scale gains could help offset mounting pressures.

Operating cash flow surged 36% to $4.4 billion, highlighting strong financial momentum. Now, all eyes are on whether rising memory and component costs will persist as hardware claims a bigger slice of sales. Cisco returned $3.7 billion to shareholders during the quarter through dividends and share buybacks, showing its capacity to generate strong cash flow while fueling growth and rewarding investors.

The $9 Billion AI Opportunity Is Not Free of Its Costs

Cisco's AI forecast depends on customers deploying systems on schedule. Management flagged optics supply as a potential constraint, while the second half of the year will test the company with tougher benchmarks. Delayed hyperscaler projects could shift revenue between quarters, and lower gross margins may limit how much sales growth reaches earnings. These risks lurk behind that bullish forecast.

Basically, HSBC is betting networking growth isn't a one-quarter spike. Its 19.2% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) forecast and $133 price target rest on the belief that AI infrastructure and broader networking demand will keep powering ahead. While some analysts have cut their price targets, they have also acknowledged the strong results and retained bullish ratings.

Cisco Must Prove It Can Keep Growth on Track

Cisco's story extends far beyond the $9 billion AI forecast. Surging networking revenue, strong orders from diverse customers, and rising guidance fuel its growth engine. The challenge is turning this demand into profitable sales while managing component costs and supply constraints. The next quarters will reveal whether Cisco can turn orders into deliveries, stabilize margins, and meet its ambitious EPS targets. If the company delivers, CSCO stock can hit HSBC's bullish target of $133 or even the Street's high price estimate of $150.

Overall, Cisco stock holds a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating on Wall Street. Of the 26 analysts covering the stock, 16 have a "Strong Buy," one has a "Moderate Buy," and nine have a "Hold" rating. The average price target sits at $129.65, suggesting a possible 37% climb, while the most bullish estimate of $150 implies potential upside of 58% from current levels.

news.Title: Nvidia vs. Intel: One AI Stock Is Worth the Drama, the Other Isn’t Worth the Wait, Says Investor
news.Content:
For a while, the only thing Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) and Intel ( NASDAQ:INTC ) had in common was that they both made chips.

Nvidia rode the AI boom to become one of the world's most valuable companies, while Intel spent years trying to repair its business. Now they share a problem: shareholders who aren't sure what comes next. Nvidia released its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, its first since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, and the stock still fell the next day. Intel's slide deepened after it issued a weak outlook in late October.

Nvidia's revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.8 billion, and interim CEO Colette Kress raised the fiscal 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%. On the same call, though, board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang. That came only hours after Huang said he would be honored to return.

Nvidia stock now hovers near its lowest level since around June 2025. This week Intel was hit by a shareholder lawsuit and by a filing showing that Nvidia sold about a quarter of its Intel stake. Intel shares sit about 60% below their June peak.

So, where to now for these two embattled chip giants?

An investor going by the moniker of The Curious Analyst (TCA) has two very different reads on these stocks.

On Nvidia, TCA thinks the leadership drama is already reflected in the share price. The stock fell sharply when Huang stepped down, but the board's refusal to bring him back drew a much milder reaction. The investor takes that as a sign the market trusts Kress. In TCA's view, investors can now see what Nvidia looks like without its founder, and the danger of relying on one person has faded.

The business case rests on the product cycle. Vera Rubin added nearly $20 billion in revenue from the previous quarter, and the investor expects growth to hold up as it ramps alongside Blackwell Ultra. TCA also expects Nvidia to use up its remaining buyback authorization of about $227 billion by the end of fiscal 2028, as management has said it will, which would shrink the share count. Assuming a net margin of about 50%, TCA's fiscal 2028 EPS estimate lands at $16.12.

Nvidia trades at roughly 10 times forward earnings, far below its historical range. TCA thinks a multiple in the low 20s, near the sector median, would be reasonable. The investor also sees an upside that the model leaves out for now. SpaceX caught Starship's upper stage for the first time last weekend, and TCA thinks cheaper launches could eventually create demand for AI hardware and data centers in space.

Story Continues

The main risks are a slowdown in AI spending and the chance that investors won't pay a higher multiple without Huang. Still, TCA notes that Nvidia impressed the market in the middle of an AI selloff and a leadership crisis, and sees that as evidence the company is on solid ground.

Bottom line, TCA reiterated a Strong Buy rating on NVDA stock. (To watch The Curious Analyst's track record, click here )

The investor is far less comfortable with Intel. Its fourth-quarter revenue guidance midpoint of $15.5 billion fell well short of the roughly $17 billion analysts expected, and the stock lost more than a quarter of its value the next day. For TCA, the bigger problem is profitability. Intel's trailing 12-month net margin is about -20%, and right now the market has little patience for cash burn.

TCA's model assumes revenue grows about 9% next year and allows for a recovery to a 6% net margin, roughly the sector median. That gives a 2027 EPS estimate of $0.78, less than half the Wall Street consensus of $1.79. The one thing TCA finds encouraging is Intel's long-term earnings growth outlook. Even so, Intel trades at about three times Nvidia's forward multiple.

The risks are more dilution after a stock sale of more than $20 billion in August, margins that could slip again, and a multiple investors may stop paying.

While TCA is no fan of the stock right now, the investor stops short of rating it a Sell. TCA argues that the post-earnings collapse already made shareholders pay for one disappointing quarter, and Intel still has a real role in PCs, data centers and AI. It has come back from tough stretches before. The investor wants to see fourth-quarter results and the 2027 outlook before deciding which way to go.

For now, TCA rates INTC stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral).

On the Street, NVDA claims a Moderate Buy consensus rating, while its $232.59 average price target points to 12-month returns of 54%. INTC is rated a Hold, although, interestingly, its $90.93 average target suggests shares will gain 66% over the one-year timeframe. (See NVDA stock forecast or INTC stock forecast )

news.Title: Apple Nears a Rare Long-Term DRAM Supply Deal With Samsung Electronics. What This Means for AAPL Stock.
news.Content:
The iPhone is selling faster, but the memory inside it is getting more expensive. Apple (AAPL) reported $57.6 billion in iPhone revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter, up 17% from a year earlier. Yet after stripping out the benefit of tariff refunds — about $2.2 billion — its gross margin fell from the prior quarter, largely because of higher memory costs.

Apple expects a gross margin of 45% to 46% in the December quarter, with higher memory costs among the factors weighing on that outlook. That makes the reported talks with Samsung Electronics over a rare deal to secure DRAM supply for several years especially timely.

Would securing more memory give Wall Street a reason to raise its earnings expectations for Apple, or would it simply help the company meet them? Let's take a closer look.

What a Samsung Deal Would Secure

Apple designs and sells iPhones, iPads, Macs, and wearables, and offers services such as iCloud, Apple Music, and Apple Pay. The company's iPhones, iPads, and Macs use dynamic random access memory (DRAM) to temporarily store the data apps need while they run.

The company is reportedly close to signing a rare multiyear deal with Samsung Electronics to secure a minimum supply of those chips. This deal would run for four to five years, starting in the first half of 2027, a departure from Apple's usual shorter contracts. Samsung would commit to supplying a minimum volume, although it is unclear how many chips that would cover. The timing helps explain why Apple is willing to commit for several years.

TrendForce, a technology market research firm, expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise 10% to 15% from the previous quarter in the final three months of 2026. That forecast reflects industry pricing rather than Apple's own costs. Meanwhile, SK Hynix (SKHY) says long-term agreements already cover more than half of its production capacity for 2027 and 2028.

The deal could help Apple keep iPhones and MacBooks in production as suppliers shift capacity toward artificial intelligence (AI) servers. It could also support the foldable iPhone Duo as Apple ramps production, although Apple hasn't identified memory as the cause of that device's supply constraints.

Story Continues

Apple's clearest potential benefit is a lower risk of lost sales from memory shortages. The catch is that securing enough chips to fill orders wouldn't protect Apple's margins if memory prices keep rising.

Where AAPL Stands Financially

Apple reported Q4 fiscal 2026 results on Nov. 2, with revenue rising 12% year-over-year (YOY) to $114.5 billion, beating the $113.6 billion consensus estimate. Its EPS of $2.10 also beat the $1.99 estimate, while gross and operating margins held steady YOY at 47.9% and 31.1%, respectively.

Apple's product revenue rose 12% to $82.9 billion, led by iPhone sales climbing 17% to $57.6 billion on strong iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro demand. Its active iPhone base hit a record, with record upgrades in the United States, China, India, and Japan.

Mac revenue rose 24% to $10.8 billion, driven by MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro demand, with room to attract first-time buyers and upgraders in emerging markets. Services revenue grew 10% YOY to $31.6 billion, supported by strength in cloud, payments, advertising, video, and music, more than 2.5 billion active devices, and more than 1.5 billion paid subscriptions.

AAPL stock fell after earnings but closed on Nov. 18 at $352.45 per share. The stock is up 29% year-to-date (YTD) and up 30% over 52 weeks.

Apple's market capitalization stands at $5.12 trillion, with a trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple and a forward P/E ratio of 39.9 times and 37.2 times, respectively, versus sector medians of about 27 times and 26 times. The forward annual dividend of $1.08 per share yields 0.31%.

CEO John Ternus flagged supply constraints and rising memory costs. The December quarter gross margin outlook of 45% to 46% reflects those higher costs and the initial Siri AI rollout expenses, per CFO Kevan Parekh. Apple sees room to expand iCloud+ and paid subscriptions, with new AI features offering another potential source of revenue.

What Analysts Expect From Apple

Wall Street expects Apple to earn $2.94 per share in the December quarter, up 3.5% from $2.84 a year earlier. Apple is expected to report those results on Feb. 4, 2027.

Analyst Dan Ives thinks investors should buy the dip. Ives argues Apple doesn't need to build data centers on the same scale as its rivals to bring AI features to the iPhone. It can lean on suppliers and cloud partners instead. He also thinks investors are underestimating how many customers will upgrade to the iPhone Duo.

Not everyone is willing to pay up for that story. Morgan Stanley rates AAPL stock as "Overweight," but its $350 price target is already below current levels. KeyBanc analyst Brandon Nispel is more skeptical. Nispel rates Apple as "Underweight" with a $250 target, citing the risk of slowing hardware sales.

That gap between ratings and price targets extends beyond those two firms. Apple has a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating from 41 analysts, yet the average target of $344.69 is about 2% below the current price of AAPL stock.

Conclusion

Apple's reported deal with Samsung would help keep iPhones shipping even if memory gets harder to buy. But with prices still tied to the market, securing chips won't shield Apple from higher costs. The most likely outcome is fewer supply headaches rather than a meaningful bump in earnings. That makes the deal good news for Apple's business, but probably not enough to lift AAPL on its own, especially with shares already trading above Wall Street's average price target.

news.Title: This Is Incredible News for AMD Stock Investors (Hint: It’s Bad News for Intel)
news.Content:
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) has been crushing Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) in the central processing unit (CPU) market, which explains why the former has been enjoying significantly stronger growth in recent quarters.

In fact, AMD is all set to become a bigger company than Intel in terms of revenue in the current quarter, and a closer look at the developments in the CPU market will tell us just why that's the case. Mercury Research, which provides data on the CPU market, recently released its third-quarter findings, which point to further gains for AMD in a lucrative space.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's take a closer look.

Image source: AMD.

AMD is becoming bigger in server CPUs

Server CPU demand has been increasing phenomenally owing to the growth in inference and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) workloads in data centers. Counterpoint Research points out that the ratio of GPU (graphics processing unit) to CPU in AI data centers has moved from 4:1 to 2:1. What's more, the firm sees a GPU to CPU ratio of 1:1 amid rising demand for agentic AI.

In simpler terms, AI data centers are now using more CPUs per GPU, leading to a phenomenal increase in the total addressable market (TAM) for server CPUs. AMD predicts that server CPU TAM will hit $220 billion in 2030, clocking annual growth of more than 50% through the end of the decade. So, AMD's rising share in this space is good news for investors.

Mercury Research points out that AMD's server CPU market share increased to 35.5% in the third quarter, a significant improvement over the year-ago period's reading of 27.8%. So, Intel lost significant ground in this market, which explains why the growth of its data center and AI (DCAI) segment was much slower than AMD's in Q3.

While AMD posted a 97% year-over-year increase in data center revenue last quarter, Intel reported a 78% increase in this segment. The gap is poised to widen in the current quarter. That's because AMD is anticipating 66% revenue growth in the current quarter to $17 billion. Intel, on the other hand, expects 13% revenue growth in the current quarter to $15.5 billion, at the midpoint of its guidance range. That's slower than the 21% revenue jump Intel delivered in Q3.

AMD can continue hurting Intel in this market

It won't be surprising to see AMD taking more market share from Intel in server CPUs next year, thanks mainly to its sixth-generation server CPUs, codenamed Venice. The company began shipping Venice processors to customers last quarter and expects a significant sales ramp next year. In the words of AMD CEO Lisa Su:

Story Continues

We began revenue shipments of EPYC Venice processors in the third quarter, and the first OEM systems are on track for availability this quarter. Early demand is the strongest we have seen for any new EPYC generation.

Our OEM and ODM partners have committed more than 240 Venice platforms, 20% more than Turin, and cloud providers are deploying Venice this quarter ahead of instance rollouts planned for early 2027.

AMD has also launched a server rack system, known as Helion, equipped with only Venice CPUs. The company points out that Helion will be offered by every major server original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and original device manufacturer (ODM) for running inference, agentic, and superintelligence workloads in the cloud

In all, Su believes that the Venice CPUs are "positioning us to gain share and significantly grow our server business." As such, I won't be surprised to see AMD's server CPU revenue jumping nicely over the next five years, driven mainly by market share gains. For instance, if AMD captures even half of the server CPU TAM in 2030, it can generate $110 billion in revenue from this segment alone (based on the $220 billion TAM estimate).

That implies a big jump in AMD's top line after four years, considering that it has generated $45 billion in revenue over the trailing twelve months. Intel, on the other hand, may continue to struggle in server CPUs and fail to keep up with AMD's rapidly improving growth trajectory. As a result, buying AMD stock over Intel seems like the logical thing to do right now, as it trades at a cheaper 31 times forward earnings compared to Chipzilla's forward price-to-earnings ratio of 32.3.

news.Title: Trump Just Disclosed Tesla and SpaceX Stock Purchases. Here's What His Portfolio Moves Reveal
news.Content:
President Donald Trump's latest stock transactions are out, and yes, Tesla and SpaceX made the list.

On Thursday, the Office of Government Ethics made public a 25-page transaction report covering hundreds of transactions from September. It shows purchases of Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) stock, along with sales of household names like McDonald's (NYSE:MCD) and Home Depot (NYSE:HD).

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

So how have the moves panned out, and what do they say about the billionaire president's portfolio? So far, the results are mixed: Several of the stocks Trump sold have outperformed the Tesla and SpaceX shares he bought, and the filing seems to indicate a shift toward dividends and bonds rather than a big bet on Elon Musk.

The Tesla and SpaceX buys were small

Reports like this one list each trade as a dollar range rather than an exact amount. Trump's four Tesla purchases, made between Sept. 1 and Sept. 10, total between $117,004 and $330,000. His two SpaceX stock purchases add up to $16,002 to $65,000. He also bought $100,001 to $250,000 in SpaceX bonds that pay 5.35% interest and mature in 2031.

The president also had much bigger moves in the filing. On Sept. 23 alone, Trump sold shares of McDonald's, Home Depot, Comcast (NASDAQ:CMCSA) and Fidelity National Information Services (NYSE:FIS) worth $1,000,001 to $5 million apiece. He also sold Nike (NYSE:NKE) and Constellation Brands (NYSE:STZ) stock worth $500,001 to $1 million each. The single largest transaction in the report, made the same day, was a purchase of $5,000,001 to $25 million of the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (NYSEMKT:VIG).

The scorecard so far

Here's how each has done since the day of the transaction, based on that day's closing price and Thursday afternoon trading, according to Nasdaq data. The filing doesn't give the exact prices Trump paid or received.

The buys:

Tesla: up about 6% since Sept. 1, the day of its largest purchase

SpaceX: down about 7% since Sept. 24, the day of its largest purchase

Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF: up about 2% since Sept. 23

The Sept. 23 sales:

Constellation Brands: up 21%

McDonald's: up 14%

Home Depot: up 13%

Comcast: up 10%

Nike: down 5%

Fidelity National Information Services: down 25%

Four of the six big stocks Trump sold have climbed 10% or more since then. But the FIS sale dodged a 25% drop, marking the best call in the batch. In other words, it's a mixed record, like most investors', and of course, these are just short-term movements. Long-term the picture can look vastly different.

Story Continues

Why copying a politician's trades is harder than it looks

There are three big problems with treating this filing as a stock-picking guide.

The first is timing. These transactions happened in September and became public about eight weeks later. Anyone who copied the McDonald's and Home Depot sales on Thursday would be selling after those stocks had already rallied.

The second is size. Because transactions are reported in ranges, a $1,001 Tesla purchase and a $15,000 one look identical. It's hard to tell a big bet from routine housekeeping.

The third is motive. The filing doesn't say who chose these transactions or why. Many of them involve funds and municipal bonds, which make the account look more like a rebalancing portfolio than a series of handpicked bets.

What investors should take away

Tesla and SpaceX are two of the most talked-about tech stocks on the market, and a presidential purchase makes a fun headline. But the biggest message in Trump's filing is a lesson in diversification: a large move into a dividend fund, trims to individual stocks, and lots of bonds.

If you like Tesla or SpaceX, buy them because you believe in the businesses and can hold through the swings, not because they showed up on a government disclosure form.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

news.Content:

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( NYSE:TSM ) and Samsung Electronics ( SSNLF ) have paused some chip shipments to China as they seek new U.S. export licenses, the Financial Times reported. The immediate concern for investors is that the restrictions reach beyond AI processors. They could also delay shipments of advanced smartphone chips and disrupt production schedules for Chinese handset makers.

The new rules, which took effect Thursday, narrow the options for Chinese companies that design their own chips and rely on overseas manufacturers to make them. Some designers had used independent packaging and testing companies to verify that their products fell outside U.S. export controls. That route is now closed for affected shipments. Washington also removed an exemption that chipmakers had used for certain products designed for non-AI uses, including smartphones.

Reuters separately reported that TSMC instructed affected customers to halt orders for chips made using 16-nanometer or more advanced technology unless they obtain export licenses. The company's guidance generally limits those customers to older 28-nanometer and 40-nanometer processes, provided the designs meet conditions covering high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging. Those two technologies are important for AI processors because they help move large amounts of data quickly between chips and memory.

The timing is difficult for Chinese companies trying to diversify their suppliers. Samsung's customers include ByteDance and Kunlun, Baidu's AI chip business, according to the Financial Times. Both have sought alternative sources for AI data centers amid shortages of Nvidia processors in China. TSMC also makes smartphone chips for Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo. Those customer relationships illustrate how the rules can affect several markets at once, though the reports did not specify which individual orders had been suspended.

Investors Takeaway

The first question is how quickly the Commerce Department approves licenses for consumer chips. An industry source told the Financial Times that smartphone chip licenses were likely to be granted, but warned that the wait could still cause manufacturing delays. For TSMC and Samsung, a short pause could primarily shift when orders ship and sales are booked. A prolonged delay could leave customers scrambling to adjust production schedules.

Story Continues

The bigger question for AI is how many advanced designs Washington will allow overseas foundries to manufacture. Chinese chip designers already face capacity constraints at domestic suppliers such as Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp. If licenses are harder to obtain for AI processors, those constraints could make it more difficult to bring alternatives to Nvidia's chips to market.

news.Content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE: TSM ) took 7th place in our list of the Top 10 Stocks to Buy According to Billionaire Ken Fisher . Ken Fisher has spent more than four decades betting that big, globally dominant companies keep winning, and his latest filing shows he still believes it. Fisher Asset Management, the firm behind Fisher Investments, reported a 13F portfolio worth about $348.3 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, up from roughly $335.8 billion three months earlier. The filing backs that optimism. Across the firm's 10 largest stock positions, Fisher added shares to every one in the third quarter. Seven of those 10 are tech, cloud or chip companies, led by the AI chip giant now dealing with the sudden exit of its founder-CEO. That concentration is a bet that AI spending, cloud growth and chip demand still have years to run. Why TSMC Made Our List Our list ranks the 10 stocks with the largest share of Fisher Asset Management's 13F portfolio for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, by the value of the fund's stake, leaving out options and ETFs. TSMC earned its spot with a stake worth $8.64 billion, or 2.48% of the portfolio. The fund held about 18.93 million shares, nearly unchanged from the prior quarter. TSMC - A Ken Fisher Stock TSMC manufactures the advanced chips that power most of the AI build-out, which makes it a way to own the boom without picking which chip designer wins. That neutrality matters more now that the leading AI chipmaker is searching for a new CEO. Demand is still accelerating. On November 10, TSMC reported October revenue of about NT$586.9 billion, up 59.7% year over year and 14.7% from September. Revenue for the first ten months of 2026 reached about NT$4.49 trillion, up 43.3% from a year earlier. Geography, alongside cost, poses the risks that generate the bearish concerns in the market. TSMC's most advanced production is concentrated in Taiwan, and building new fabs in the U.S. and elsewhere is expensive. Also, if there were to be any slowdown in AI orders, it would hit its fastest-growing lines first. Ken Fisher has spent more than four decades betting that big, globally dominant companies keep winning, and his latest filing shows he still believes it. Fisher Asset Management, the firm behind Fisher Investments, reported a 13F portfolio worth about $348.3 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, up from roughly $335.8 billion three months earlier.

Fisher founded his firm in 1979, wrote a Forbes column for more than 32 years, and has authored 11 books. Today he serves as executive chairman and co-chief investment officer. His market call heading into the midterms was unambiguous. In an October interview, he said midterm years kick off what he considers the most consistently positive nine-month stretch in U.S. stock market history, because political gridlock blocks controversial legislation. In his words,

The stock markets celebrate when major bills fall through.

The filing backs that optimism. Across the firm's 10 largest stock positions, Fisher added shares to every one in the third quarter, from a 0.3% top-up in an industrial bellwether to a 7% increase in a weight-loss drug leader. Seven of those 10 are tech, cloud or chip companies, led by the AI chip giant now dealing with the sudden exit of its founder-CEO. The notable cut came in bonds: Fisher trimmed his 7-10 year Treasury bond fund by about 22%, to roughly 126 million shares, a move consistent with a manager leaning into stocks rather than hiding in bonds. Together, the top 10 stocks make up about a third of the portfolio.

That concentration is a bet that AI spending, cloud growth and chip demand still have years to run. It also means the portfolio will feel any AI slowdown more than most. Microsoft is Fisher's AI holding with the clearest line of sight to revenue. Azure rents AI capacity to businesses, and much of that demand is already under contract.

news.Title: Cerebras Drops 20% in a Month: Is the Stock a Buy on the Dip?

The company continues to face stiff competition from NVIDIA NVDA, Advanced Micro Devices AMD and Intel INTC in the AI space. CBRS' Prospects Suffer From Data Center Delays

Concerns surrounding Cerebras' relationship with OpenAI have been a major overhang on its shares. During the third-quarter 2026 earnings call, Cerebras acknowledged that insufficient data center capacity prevented a broader rollout of OpenAI's Ultrafast offerings. CBRS management, however, rejected speculation that technical limitations were responsible and reiterated that OpenAI remains an important customer. The company disclosed delays in delivering portions of the contracted 750 megawatts of inference capacity, primarily due to land, power and building infrastructure constraints. Cerebras expects to return to its planned delivery schedule by the second half of 2027.

Profitability remains another concern for Cerebras. Despite reporting record third-quarter 2026 revenues, GAAP gross margin contracted to 20% from 40.6% in the year-ago quarter, reflecting a weaker hardware margin profile and accounting adjustments. Core hardware gross margin was 31%, pressured by shipments under older, lower-priced contracts. Meanwhile, the company reported a GAAP net loss of $161.2 million compared with $22.2 million in the prior-year quarter.

Cerebras' prospects are suffering from stiff competition from the likes of NVIDIA (NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Intel (INTC) in the AI space. NVIDIA is dominating the AI GPU market through its Blackwell, Hopper and DGX/NVL systems that are used for AI training and inference. AMD's MI300 and MI350 accelerator families are competing with CBRS in hyperscale AI infrastructure and enterprise AI clusters. Meanwhile, Intel's Gaudi AI accelerators target enterprise AI training and inference as a lower-cost GPU alternative. Shares of AMD, NVIDIA and Intel have dropped 0.8%, 30.2% and 40.4%, respectively, over the past month.

Cerebras' expanding product portfolio and differentiated wafer-scale computing architecture remain important competitive advantages. The company's CS-4 AI accelerator is approaching full production and is expected to double the performance and throughput of CS-3. The next-generation CS-5 system, powered by Wafer Scale Engine 5, is targeted for production in early summer 2027 and is designed to deliver more than twice the speed of CS-4. Cerebras has also introduced production-scale heterogeneous disaggregated inference using AMD GPUs alongside its proprietary systems. Unlike competing GPU architectures, Cerebras' systems do not require high-bandwidth memory, reducing exposure to memory shortages and associated cost inflation.

news.Title: Prediction: SpaceX Will Be the Largest Company in the World by 2040
news.Content:
Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) is already the sixth-most valuable company in the world, with a market capitalization approaching $2 trillion. Not too shabby, considering the company just went public in June at a valuation of about $1.8 trillion.

But I think we're only seeing the beginning of what this company could become.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Here's my prediction: By 2040, SpaceX will be the largest company in the world, surpassing Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG)(NASDAQ:GOOGL), and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN). And my prediction hinges on three things.

1. SpaceX and Tesla will merge

SpaceX had barely finished its IPO when longtime Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) bull Dan Ives put the chances of SpaceX and Tesla merging within a year at 80%. And why not? Elon Musk is the CEO of both companies, and both are focused on developing artificial intelligence and bringing new products to market. They even collaborate to some extent.

In October, Musk himself lent those rumors even more credibility when he announced that both companies had formed merger-exploration committees . Because of the inherent conflict of interest created by his massive equity stakes in the two companies, Musk isn't a member of those committees — but the effort wouldn't be happening without his blessing.

I previously projected that a combined SpaceX-Tesla company would be worth more than $5 trillion by 2029 . SpaceX has AI computing infrastructure, satellite communications, and rocket technology. Tesla adds electric vehicles, autonomous driving systems, robotics, and manufacturing capabilities.

Image source: Getty Images.

The combined company would be much more efficient, as it could develop advanced AI models, train them on its own computing infrastructure, and deploy that intelligence across Tesla's vehicles and robots.

The merger isn't guaranteed, and Tesla shareholders would need to be satisfied with the terms. But I believe it will happen.

2. SpaceX will develop the enterprise AI market

SpaceX's rocket launch business and Starlink satellite broadband service are impressive. But I don't think there's any question that AI is the company's biggest growth opportunity. In its IPO prospectus, SpaceX identified a total addressable market of $28.5 trillion for itself, which it said was the largest in human history. And of that, $22.7 trillion involves enterprise AI applications.

Story Continues

While the figure represents the potential market, and not revenue SpaceX is guaranteed to capture, even a relatively small share could become an enormous business. And SpaceX is already making plenty of headway. Its revenue in the third quarter was $14.6 billion, with the AI division generating $7.6 billion of that sum. That segment brought in just $813 million in the same quarter a year ago.

The division also recorded $431 million in operating income, reversing a $1.7 billion operating loss from the prior-year period.

SpaceX ended September with 1.7 gigawatts of installed computing capacity, and Musk has indicated that demand for the company's AI infrastructure substantially exceeds its available supply. But while renting computing power to other companies is a nice business, the real opportunity lies in SpaceX developing AI models and applications that could eventually compete for enterprise customers.

If Musk and Co. can turn even a fraction of that $22.7 trillion opportunity into recurring revenue, a $10 trillion valuation starts looking considerably more realistic.

3. Tesla will monetize its Optimus robots

Tesla is the most valuable automaker in the world and gets most of its revenue from its electric vehicles, but it is a company in transition. This year, it stopped production of its Model X and Model S vehicles to free up manufacturing capacity for the Optimus robot, and it's also halting Cybertruck production with the plan of converting those lines to make its autonomous Cybercabs.

The Optimus robot has the potential to be a big winner for Tesla. Musk describes it as a humanoid robot capable of performing tasks in factories, warehouses, and homes. Musk believes robotics could become Tesla's most important business, surpassing electric vehicles.

It plans to manufacture second-generation Optimus robots at its Texas Gigafactory, with a stated annual production capacity of 10 million units.

I don't know if we'll ever see those kinds of numbers for Optimus. But I do think the robotics business can be a growth driver if Tesla proves its robots can reliably perform useful tasks at a price customers will accept.

But imagine the opportunity if Optimus succeeds. A combined SpaceX-Tesla could develop the AI systems that power these robots, manufacture them at enormous scale, and potentially sell both the hardware and supporting software.

SpaceX's path to becoming the biggest company in the world

SpaceX isn't going to become the world's most valuable company simply by launching more rockets or adding more Starlink subscribers. But if it joins forces with Tesla, seizes a portion of the huge enterprise AI market, and turns a profit with Optimus, it's hard to see any other company matching up.

If Musk can pull this off, then his next 14 years could make his first two decades at Tesla and SpaceX look like the opening act.

news.Title: Not AMD. Not Intel. This Is the Chip Stock Wall Street Is Underestimating
news.Content:
So far, there are surely many investors who want to put November behind them. Companies like Nvidia are among those having a rough month, considering the tech stock sell-off, the backlash against data centers, and a scandal that cost Jensen Huang his job as CEO .

Understandably, some shareholders are getting a little nervous. And if you're looking for another way to invest in artificial intelligence, there are certainly options. Advanced Micro Devices and Intel are two obvious candidates, but I think Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) deserves a lot more love than it's getting.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

On Nov. 13, Rothschild & Co Redburn downgraded Broadcom stock from "Buy" to "Neutral" and cut its price target from $595 to $398. That's nearly $200 wiped off the analyst's expectations in one shot.

But hold the phone: Broadcom's revenue is growing at a rapid pace. Its AI business is exploding, and it's generating billions in cash. Even so, the stock price is essentially in 2026. Let's see what's going on.

Image source: Getty Images.

Take a look at these numbers

Broadcom's revenue for its fiscal third quarter (ended Aug. 2) was $29.6 billion, up 86% from a year ago. And its AI semiconductor business did even better, generating $16.7 billion in revenue, an incredible 221% increase.

The chipmaker doesn't expect things to slow down, either. Management issued guidance for $21.7 billion in AI semiconductor revenue in the fourth quarter, up another 236% from a year ago.

Broadcom competes with Nvidia in the AI accelerator space, but it takes a different tack. While Nvidia's all-powerful graphics processing units can do pretty much anything that a company needs to train and run AI programs, Broadcom's custom AI accelerators are chips designed around the specific needs of large technology customers.

If companies want to build their own AI chips rather than relying entirely on Nvidia, Broadcom is one company they can turn to for that purpose.

Broadcom generated $13.7 billion in free cash flow in the third quarter, compared with $7 billion a year earlier. That means the company nearly doubled its cash generation while growing revenue by 86%. What's not to like?

But what about that downgrade?

Rothschild & Co Redburn points out that Broadcom is counting heavily on companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to keep spending enormous sums on AI infrastructure. And neither AI start-up has demonstrated that it can sustain that spending from its own cash generation.

Story Continues

Anthropic recently announced a $63 billion financing arrangement to fund computing infrastructure powered by Broadcom's custom AI chips and networking technology. Broadcom also has financial exposure to Anthropic's ability to meet some of its obligations.

That's a pretty substantial bet on a company that's still losing money. But investors should also recognize that Broadcom has more going for it than AI chips.

Its infrastructure software business, which includes VMware, generated $8.75 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 29% year over year. That's nearly 30% of Broadcom's total business, and it gives the company another way to make money from businesses investing in their computing infrastructure.

Broadcom is also bringing AI capabilities to VMware, including tools that allow companies to run AI applications in private cloud environments. So while the biggest AI developers get the headlines, Broadcom is selling technology to a much wider group of customers.

Is Broadcom stock worth buying?

I wouldn't ignore the risks involving Anthropic and OpenAI. If their spending plans unravel, Broadcom could have a serious problem. And the stock isn't immune to the broader pullback in AI investments.

But Broadcom's business is delivering results right now. Revenue is soaring, free cash flow is growing, and its custom chips have become an important alternative to Nvidia's processors.

Investors will get another update when Broadcom reports earnings on Dec. 9. With the stock essentially flat this year, I think there's a compelling argument that Wall Street is paying too much attention to what could go wrong and not enough to what's already going right.

news.Title: Amkor's Computing Business Gains Momentum: Is More Growth Ahead?

Amkor Technology AMKR is positioned for sustained Computing revenue growth through 2027 as artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure demand accelerates and advanced packaging programs scale. In third-quarter 2026, Computing revenues surged 37% year over year and 25% sequentially to a record, lifting the segment's share of total sales to 26% from 19% a year earlier. This growing contribution highlights Computing's increasing importance to Amkor's revenue mix.

The momentum reflects the ongoing ramp of Amkor's flagship high-density fan-out (HDFO) CPU program and the start of an additional HDFO CPU program for a hyperscaler in third-quarter 2026. Two 2.5D programs for networking and data centers were expected to begin ramping in the fourth quarter, broadening its exposure beyond traditional CPUs. The company expects Computing revenues to grow at a low-double-digit rate sequentially in the fourth quarter, translating to more than 50% year-over-year growth.

Looking further ahead, management projected more than 30% Computing growth in 2026 and a similar or higher rate in 2027. Expansion in Korea, including two new buildings at Gwangju and additional test capacity at Songdo, should support data center demand. Long-term capacity commitments and advance customer payments also provide greater visibility into future production needs.

However, weaker PC demand and elevated memory costs could limit growth; meanwhile, the complex, more-than-300-step HDFO production process creates ramp-up execution risks. Heavy investments in new capacity may also increase depreciation and pressure margins if utilization falls short of expectations. Yet, robust AI-related demand, new program ramps and growing capacity support a favorable Computing revenue outlook through 2027.

How Do the Competitors Compare to AMKR?

Intel INTC competes with Amkor through its advanced semiconductor packaging capabilities targeting AI and high-performance computing. Intel's Foveros 3D stacking and Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge (EMIB) technologies enable complex chiplet integration, competing with Amkor's HDFO and 2.5D solutions. Intel is expanding its advanced packaging capabilities in New Mexico to attract external foundry customers, strengthening its position in AI infrastructure.

GlobalFoundries GFS competes with Amkor through advanced packaging, heterogeneous integration and 2.5D/3D technologies. GlobalFoundries is expanding its U.S. packaging ecosystem through a $2 billion multiyear agreement with TSMC to manufacture silicon interposers for AI and high-performance computing applications. news.Title: 174-year-old American bank’s Bitcoin exposure nears Tesla and SpaceX
news.Content:
When people think of big Bitcoin holders, they usually picture tech companies, not a traditional bank. Wells Fargo's latest filing suggests that picture may need updating.

Wells Fargo reported 49,577,094 shares of BlackRock 's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, according to its quarterly 13F filing .

The stake was worth about $2.35 billion, spread across five lines from different parts of the bank.

IBIT is an exchange-traded fund that holds Bitcoin directly and trades like a stock. Each share represents a small slice of the fund's Bitcoin.

Related: Analyst warns Anthropic IPO is pulling money out of Bitcoin

About 28,000 Bitcoin, indirectly

IBIT held 801,033 Bitcoin against 1,414,760,000 shares outstanding on Sept. 30, according to its quarterly report .

At that ratio, Wells Fargo's shares equal about 28,070 Bitcoin.

Tesla held 11,509 Bitcoin as of Sept. 30, bought for $386 million, according to its quarterly report .

SpaceX held 18,712 Bitcoin, according to its IPO filing , the same amount it reported at the end of both 2024 and 2025. Together, the two companies hold 30,221 Bitcoin.

That puts Wells Fargo's exposure at about 93% of the two companies' combined holdings. It already tops either one on its own.

A stake that grew all year

The holding grew fast.

At the end of March, Wells Fargo reported about 6.5 million IBIT shares, worth roughly $250 million, according to an amended filing for that quarter.

By the end of June, that had grown to 24,396,222 shares, worth about $812.2 million, according to its June filing .

AI-linked tokens tumble as doubts emerge over tech boom

Its share count then about doubled again by September, and the value nearly tripled as Bitcoin rose during the quarter.

Wells Fargo also reported options on IBIT: puts covering 540,000 shares and calls covering 717,200. A put profits if a price falls, and a call profits if it rises.

Mostly clients, not the bank

The headline number comes with a big caveat. 13F filings include shares held for clients through brokerage and advisory accounts, not just the bank's own money.

The filing doesn't show how much belongs to Wells Fargo itself.

In practice, that makes this less a story about a bank buying Bitcoin and more about its customers, who are using ETFs to get Bitcoin exposure inside traditional accounts.

The figures reflect positions on Sept. 30, before Bitcoin's sharp fall. Bitcoin traded at $63,058 at 18:18 UTC on Nov. 18, according to Decibel , well below its quarter-end level.

Factors to Influence HPE's Q4 Results

Hewlett Packard Enterprise's fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 performance is likely to have benefited from accelerating demand for AI infrastructure, traditional servers and networking solutions. The company's Cloud & AI business is expected to have remained a key growth driver, with management projecting revenue growth of 60-72% in the to-be-reported quarter. Increasing enterprise investments in AI inferencing, agentic AI and data-intensive workloads should support demand for HPE's server and storage portfolio.

AI infrastructure adoption is expanding beyond pilot projects toward production deployments. HPE's AI systems orders reached $2.4 billion in the third quarter, while its AI systems backlog increased 14% sequentially to $6.8 billion. The company's $3.5 billion hyperscaler inferencing deal and expanding Private Cloud AI adoption are likely to have supported revenue conversion in the fourth quarter. Its AI Factory solutions, developed in collaboration with NVIDIA, might have strengthened its position in enterprise AI infrastructure.

Networking is another important growth catalyst. HPE's acquisition of Juniper Networks has expanded its presence across data center switching, routing, campus and branch networking. Networks for AI orders reached $700 million in the third quarter, while normalized networking orders increased 36%. Continued demand for AI networking infrastructure and integration synergies should support the segment, with management expecting fourth-quarter networking revenue growth of 11-13%.

GreenLake and HPE's hybrid cloud portfolio should also contribute to performance. Its consumption-based model, alongside Morpheus and OpsRamp capabilities, enables customers to manage hybrid IT environments and increasingly complex AI workloads. Rising GreenLake adoption and demand for Alletra storage and Private Cloud AI could have strengthened recurring customer relationships.

Investment Thesis for HPE Stock

Hewlett Packard Enterprise is aligning compute, storage and networking with enterprise inferencing, agentic AI and data intensive workloads. HPE's server portfolio includes general-purpose and workload-optimized systems, high-performance computing, supercomputing, AI infrastructure, data analytics and transaction processing. Its storage offerings include HPE Alletra, unstructured data solutions, data protection, GreenLake Flex and related software. The segment is benefiting from growing demand for AI-ready servers and enterprise infrastructure.

HPE competes with Super Micro Computer SMCI, Dell Technologies DELL and Cisco CSCO in the AI infrastructure market. However, HPE's ability to package compute, storage, networking and services into pre-configured solutions can reduce deployment complexity for enterprises and sovereign customers while giving it an edge over its competitors. Super Micro Computer is on track to scale rack production capacity to more than 6,000 AI racks per month by the end of fiscal 2026, including 3,000 direct liquid cooling racks monthly.

Super Micro Computer is already shipping 150kW AI racks in volume and preparing 250kW and 500kW rack solutions to support future high-density AI training and inference workloads. Dell Technologies is a major supplier of servers and storage systems, with a broad customer base across enterprises and cloud providers. Its scale, established distribution and service offerings give it an edge in winning large contracts.

Cisco closed fiscal 2026 with $9.3 billion in hyperscaler AI infrastructure orders, about 4.5 times fiscal 2025, and roughly $4 billion in related revenues. However, HPE's ability to package compute, storage, networking and services into pre-configured solutions can reduce deployment complexity for enterprises and sovereign customers. This gives HPE an edge over its competitors.

Conclusion: Buy HPE Stock Now

HPE's expanding AI infrastructure portfolio, strong networking demand and growing hybrid cloud adoption position it for continued growth. Record AI backlog, Juniper integration synergies and improving cash generation support its long-term outlook. While supply constraints and potential margin moderation remain concerns, HPE's growth opportunities and attractive valuation support a positive investment thesis.

news.Title: Why It’s Time to Buy the Pullback in Qualcomm Stock
news.Content:
Qualcomm (QCOM) stock has been under pressure, declining more than 38% from its 52-week high. The loss of Apple (AAPL) revenue and the adverse impact of rising memory costs on its handset business have weighed on its revenue and profitability.

The impact is evident in the company's fiscal 2026 results. Qualcomm reported revenue of $43.1 billion, down 3% from $44.3 billion in fiscal 2025. The company's core Qualcomm CDMA Technologies (QCT) business also saw revenue decline 3% year-over-year (YOY), largely due to weaker handset sales. However, strength in the automotive and Internet of Things (IoT) businesses supported its top line, while revenue from its Qualcomm Technology Licensing (QTL) segment remained broadly flat.

Profitability also took a hit. Adjusted EPS fell 12% YOY to $12.03 in fiscal 2026, reflecting weaker handset performance and continued margin pressure.

Despite these near-term challenges, there are reasons to remain optimistic about Qualcomm's prospects. Much of the negative news is already reflected in the price of QCOM stock. At the same time, its growing pipeline of opportunities across automotive, IoT, data center, and other markets provides a solid base for growth.

Qualcomm Is Set for Stronger Growth

Qualcomm entered fiscal 2027 strong, supported by its strategic shift toward revenue diversification, a solid data-center revenue opportunity, and ongoing strength in automotive.

Qualcomm expects non-handset revenues within its QCT segment — which is comprised of automotive, IoT, and data center — to increase by more than 60% YOY. These businesses are also projected to contribute more than 50% of total QCT revenues during the fiscal year, highlighting Qualcomm's gradual transition away from its traditional dependence on the smartphone market.

The data-center business is expected to become a significant growth contributor as Qualcomm moves from customer engagements to commercial shipments. Management has reaffirmed its revenue targets of $5 billion for fiscal 2027 and $15 billion for fiscal 2029, with the business expected to exit fiscal 2027 at an annualized revenue run rate (ARR) of approximately $7 billion. Initial shipments to two hyperscaler customers are expected to help generate more than $650 million in data-center revenue in the December quarter.

Story Continues

Furthermore, Qualcomm's strategic agreement with Amazon's (AMZN) Amazon Web Services presents a revenue opportunity of up to $60 billion over the next decade, while additional engagements with hyperscalers could further strengthen its long-term growth pipeline.

Qualcomm's automotive business is also demonstrating strong momentum, achieving an $8 billion ARR by the end of fiscal 2026. At the same time, investments in agentic artificial intelligence (AI), AI accelerators, and CPU platforms are positioning the company to capitalize on emerging computing requirements and create new product opportunities.

In QTL, Qualcomm has completed long-term agreements with major customers, including Apple, Huawei, and Transsion. These renewals provide greater revenue visibility and reduce near-term licensing uncertainty, while management expects the long-term QTL revenue outlook to remain unchanged. Additionally, planned product price increases to offset higher semiconductor input costs are expected to support QCT gross margins, with the full benefits likely to materialize in the second half of fiscal 2027.

Overall, Qualcomm's prospects remain solid, driven by a structural shift toward a more diversified revenue base. Expanding data-center operations, resilient automotive demand, AI-related investments, and stable licensing revenues provide multiple growth drivers.

Qualcomm's Diversified Growth Story Makes the Pullback Worth Buying

Wall Street analysts have a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating for QCOM stock. However, the pullback presents an attractive opportunity for long-term investors, as Qualcomm's growth prospects extend well beyond the challenged smartphone market. Although the loss of Apple-related revenue, weaker handset demand, and rising memory costs have weighed on its recent financial performance, the company's expanding automotive, IoT, and data-center businesses offer meaningful growth opportunities.

Moreover, renewed licensing agreements and planned product price increases should provide additional support to revenue visibility and margins. While near-term volatility may persist, Qualcomm's expanding growth pipeline and strategic positioning in AI infrastructure strengthen its investment case.

news.Title: Analysts Turned Bullish on These 5 Stocks on Tuesday
news.Content:
Wall Street is trading on what the Federal Reserve does next, even as analysts keep changing their ratings. The Fed held its key rate steady at its October 27 to 28 meeting, after raising it in September for the first time in three years.

Minutes released on November 18 showed that nearly all officials expect a quarter-point increase in December, and two raised the idea of a half-point move. Wall Street puts the odds of a December hike near 95%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

The jump in expectations began on November 10, when a hotter-than-expected October inflation report sent the 2-year Treasury yield up more than 18 basis points, its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, Reuters reported.

Why the Fed May Not Be Done Raising Rates

Fed Governor Christopher Waller backs the larger move. He said inflation is "headed in the wrong direction and it's spreading out," and he put core inflation at about a 3.5% annual rate over the past three months, against the Fed's 2% target. Readers following analysts' favorite growth names can find more in our ranking of aggressive growth picks from Wall Street analysts .

New York Fed President John Williams disagrees and does not think the situation calls for dramatic action. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has said the economy will likely need several rate increases before spring 2027, and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly leans toward more hikes because she worries that companies are passing higher costs on to consumers.

Treasury Yields Back Above 5% Draw Investor Attention

The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.36% on October 7, its highest level in regular trading since 2002, and it was on pace on November 17 for its 27th close above 5% this year, Bloomberg reported. All of 2007 had 29 such closes. Analysts are still finding value at these levels, as our list of affordable stocks to buy according to Wall Street analysts shows.

JPMorgan Asset Management portfolio manager Priya Misra said yields above 5% reflect a "risk premium due to uncertainty about the Fed." Dan Carter of Fort Washington Investment Advisors said fixed income offers better risk and reward than it has in some time, and that the stock rally since 2023 may push many portfolios to rebalance toward bonds. The pressure is also showing up in housing: 30-year mortgage rates have stayed above 7% since mid-September, and Ian Lyngen of BMO Capital Markets said the effect on real estate has been to freeze activity.

We shared the expanded list of Analysts Turned Bullish on These 10 Stocks on Tuesday here. You can find the top 5 stocks below.

Story Continues

Our Methodology

To compile this list, we reviewed analyst rating upgrades and price target increases announced on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. We selected 10 stocks that are listed in the U.S. and had an analyst call that day, and ranked them in ascending order of their average upside potential. Upside is based on analysts' average price target compared with each stock's share price, as of November 18.

At Insider Monkey, we are obsessed with what hedge funds do. The reason is simple: our research has shown that we can outperform the market by imitating the top stock picks of the best hedge funds. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 612% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 375 percentage points ( see more details here ).

Analysts Turned Bullish on These 5 Stocks on Tuesday

5. Nucor (NYSE:NUE)

Average Upside Potential: 23%

Morgan Stanley upgraded Nucor to Overweight from Equalweight on November 17 and raised its price target to $310 from $300, pointing to lower capital spending.

Nucor makes steel and steel products through three segments: steel mills, steel products and raw materials. In the third quarter of 2026, it earned $5.80 per diluted share on net sales of $11.25 billion, up from $2.63 per share a year earlier, and steel mill shipments reached 7,231 thousand tons, up from 6,428 thousand tons a year earlier. Over the first nine months of 2026, free cash flow came to $2.66 billion, and the company returned cash to shareholders, much of it through share repurchases.

Nucor's new sheet mill in West Virginia had its first heat in September. In Morgan Stanley's view, lower capital spending leaves more cash for buybacks and dividends. Nucor reported those results on October 26 and said it expects fourth-quarter earnings to be in line with or modestly higher than the third quarter. Our piece on Nucor's strong shipments and the questions around its third-quarter guidance covers the debate over that outlook.

4. Humana (NYSE:HUM)

Average Upside Potential: 32%

Bernstein raised its price target on Humana to $515 from $425 on November 17 and kept its Outperform rating. The firm said stable medical use and industry pricing discipline support a recovery in Medicare Advantage margins.

Humana sells Medicare Advantage and other health insurance plans and runs the CenterWell care business. In the third quarter of 2026, Humana reported GAAP earnings of $1.33 per share but an adjusted loss of $0.70 per share, against adjusted earnings of $3.24 a year earlier, as revenue grew. Humana reported those results on November 6, 2026. It raised its 2026 adjusted earnings guidance to at least $9.50.

On November 18, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposed a rule that would tighten oversight of Medicare, Medicaid and the health insurance marketplace, with more audits of insurers and a way for the agency to recover improper payments, and Humana was among the insurers whose shares fell. Public comment on the proposal is open until January 19, 2027. We wrote about how Humana expects most of its members to be in four-star plans before that.

3. M-tron Industries (NYSEAMERICAN:MPTI)

Average Upside Potential: 34%

Freedom Broker analyst Sergey Glinyanov upgraded M-tron Industries to Buy from Hold on November 17 even as he cut his price target to $84 from $88, citing "lower valuation multiples and a higher discount rate." He still raised his estimates for 2026 through 2028, with the biggest increase in 2028 on missile programs for Raytheon and Lockheed Martin.

M-tron makes frequency and spectrum control products, such as oscillators and filters, for aerospace and defense customers. Revenue in the third quarter of 2026 rose to $15.7 million, and backlog stood at $84.9 million on September 30, up from the end of 2025. M-tron reported those results on November 12, before Freedom Broker moved to Buy.

Glinyanov expects 2027 to be a transition year, with costs for added capacity and new hires weighing on results. He also sees the company's radar business growing from under $2 million to about $8 million a year. Management cautioned that backlog could dip in the fourth quarter, which Freedom Broker attributed to contract timing rather than weaker demand. Freedom Broker also called the September 30 backlog a record high.

2. Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO)

Average Upside Potential: 35%

HSBC upgraded Cisco to Buy from Hold on November 17 and raised its price target to $133 from $120, pointing to growth in AI networking.

Cisco designs and sells the networking equipment and software that connect company and cloud data centers. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, revenue rose 24% from a year earlier, and Chief Executive Officer Chuck Robbins said, "We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking supercycle." The company expects $9 billion in AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers in fiscal 2027, more than double the total for fiscal 2026. Product revenue grew faster than total revenue in the first quarter, which ended on October 24, 2026.

Robbins, who spoke when the company reported on November 12, also said the quarter brought Cisco's strongest revenue and earnings per share growth in more than 15 years, and the company raised its fiscal 2027 non-GAAP earnings per share guidance to $5.47 to $5.53. Our analysis of whether Cisco can profit from helping customers spend less on AI takes up the other side of that demand.

1. Praxis Precision Medicines (NASDAQ:PRAX)

Average Upside Potential: 120%

Wells Fargo analyst Ben Burnett upgraded Praxis Precision Medicines to Overweight from Equal Weight on November 17 and raised his price target to $509 from $343. He said the company's investor day on November 12 had eased his concerns about the endpoint in its ulixacaltamide trial.

Praxis develops treatments for brain disorders such as essential tremor and rare genetic forms of epilepsy. The FDA's target decision date for relutrigine, which treats two types of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, is December 27, 2026, and the date for ulixacaltamide, for essential tremor, is January 29, 2027. Chief Executive Officer Marcio Souza said, "We are entering a defining period for Praxis, with two key regulatory milestones ahead."

The company ended the third quarter of 2026 with about $1.3 billion in cash and investments, which it expects to fund operations into 2028. Its net loss widened to $94.2 million from $73.9 million a year earlier, and the company also expects results from its EMERALD trial in the fourth quarter of 2026. Praxis said the relutrigine team is fully hired and that it expects the ulixacaltamide sales force to be in place in the fourth quarter of 2026.

While we acknowledge the risk and potential of PRAX as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. news.Title: Why It’s Time to Buy the Pullback in Intel Stock
news.Content:
Intel (INTC) stock has witnessed a steep correction, eroding a substantial portion of its year-to-date (YTD) gains. INTC stock has fallen more than 61% from its 52-week high and about 39% over the past month.

Multiple factors have dragged Intel stock down, including disappointing fourth-quarter revenue guidance, manufacturing capacity constraints, rising memory prices, tighter corporate IT budgets, and broader weakness across artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks. These challenges are significant for Intel's Client Computing business, where demand conditions have weakened considerably.

More News from Barchart
